propositions.text: I allow this appeal.
propositions.quote: I allow this appeal.

propositions.text: The appellants are Mexican citizens named PA, AA, and minors.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant, "PA") and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellant, "AA"), XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Minor Appellants) are citizens of Mexico.

propositions.text: The appellants fear harm from Cartel del Noreste linked to Los Zetas; PA was threatened with extortion and death, refused, reported to police, then went into hiding after threats and attempt on life.
propositions.quote: The Appellants fear harm from the Cartel del Noreste, a cartel associated with the Zetas. The PA was threatened with extortion and death if he did not comply. He refused to comply and filed a formal report to the Federal Police group that was working with the Drug Enforcement Agency. After receiving threats, being followed and an attempt on the PA's life, the Appellants went into hiding.

propositions.text: The police commander who helped PA was murdered and the PA's report disappeared.
propositions.quote: The Commander who assisted the PA with his report on extortion was murdered and there is no longer any trace of the report the PA made.

propositions.text: The RPD found appellants credible, PA targeted for extortion by criminals linked to Treasury Office agent, but insufficient evidence that cartel was agent of harm or that formal investigation occurred; RPD found viable internal flight alternative (IFA).
propositions.quote: The RPD found the Appellants credible and concluded that the PA was targeted for extortion by criminals associated with an agent at the Treasury Office. There was insufficient evidence to conclude that a cartel was the agent of harm. There was also insufficient evidence that there was a formal investigation based on the PA's report. The RPD determined that the Appellants had a viable internal flight alternative (IFA) in Merida or Campeche.

propositions.text: The appellants argue the RPD erred by not considering objective country documentation consistent with PA's narrative.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the RPD erred by not considering objective country documentation that is consistent with the PA's narrative.

propositions.text: The determinative issue is internal flight alternative (IFA).
propositions.quote: The determinative issue is IFA.

propositions.text: I find appellants do not have an IFA in Merida, Campeche, or elsewhere; objective evidence shows likely harm by agent of harm anywhere in Mexico.
propositions.quote: I find the Appellants do not have an IFA in Merida, Campeche, or elsewhere in Mexico. Objective evidence establishes, on a balance of probabilities, that it is likely the agent of harm could locate and harm the Appellants in Mexico.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal, finds appellants are Mexican citizens fearing harm from Cartel del Noreste linked to Los Zetas, that the RPD found them credible but erred on IFA, and the court finds no IFA exists.

propositions.text: The appeal is allowed and I substitute my own decision that appellants are persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The appeal is allowed. I substitute my own decision that the Appellants are persons in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal and substitutes its own decision that appellants need protection.

propositions.text: PA testified extortion attempt began after registering used auto business at Treasury Office; he was followed, threatened, and refused to pay extortion.
propositions.quote: The PA testified that the attempt to extort his business arose after he attempted to register his used auto sales business at a government Treasury Office. He began to receive phone calls and was followed and chased by a car. He and his wife began to suspect they were under surveillance at their home. The PA received a phone call in which he was told they knew about his auto sales business and ordered him to pay money on a monthly basis or he would face consequences. He refused.

propositions.text: Appellants spoke with police commander related to AA, who said extortion was by cartel linked to Los Zetas; commander helped find lawyer to file complaint.
propositions.quote: The Appellants spoke with a police commander who was married to the AA's cousin. He told them it was extortion by a cartel linked to the Los Zetas cartel. The commander assisted the PA in finding a brave lawyer who helped him to file a complaint to the police about the extortion attempt.

propositions.text: Appellants went into hiding during investigation; later learned cartel sought them; commander was murdered; complaint file disappeared.
propositions.quote: The Appellants were advised to go into hiding while the complaint was investigated and they did so. Several months later, the Appellants learned they were being sought after by the cartel. They subsequently found out that the commander had been murdered. Their lawyer advised them to leave the country. The Appellants were later informed by their lawyer that the PA's complaint file had disappeared.

paragraphs.summary: The PA testified about extortion attempts, help from a police commander and lawyer, hiding, threats, murder of commander, and disappearance of complaint file.

propositions.text: My role is to review all evidence and decide if RPD made correct decision.
propositions.quote: My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.

propositions.text: It is more likely than not that appellants will be located and harmed in Mexico.
propositions.quote: It is more likely than not that the Appellants will be located and harmed in Mexico

paragraphs.summary: The court states its role to review evidence and finds appellants likely to be located and harmed in Mexico.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD erred by finding insufficient evidence that cartel could locate appellants in Merida or Campeche and was selective in reviewing country documentation.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in determining that there was insufficient evidence that a cartel had the capacity to locate the Appellants in Merida or Campeche. They argue that the RPD was selective in its review of the country documentation regarding the current context of regional cartels in Mexico and the capacity to track someone in Mexico.

propositions.text: Appellants argue objective country documentation supports their credible testimony.
propositions.quote: They further argue there is objective country documentation that supports the Appellants' testimony, which was found to be credible by the RPD.

propositions.text: I agree that extortion and threats were committed by cartel linked to Los Zetas.
propositions.quote: I agree. The extortion and threats of harm were committed by a cartel with links to Los Zetas

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue RPD erred by ignoring evidence that cartels can locate them; court agrees extortion was by cartel linked to Los Zetas.

propositions.text: RPD found PA and AA credible and forthright; PA targeted for extortion by criminals linked to Treasury Office agent; insufficient evidence of formal police investigation or foul play in complaint disappearance.
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that the PA and AA gave consistent and forthright testimony and found them to be credible. The RPD found that the PA was targeted for extortion by criminals associated with the government agent at the Treasury Office, but found there was insufficient evidence to determine that a formal investigation was carried out by Mexico police based on the PA's complaint. The RPD found there was no evidence that the complaint investigation disappeared from the system due to foul play or maliciously by any agent of harm.

propositions.text: RPD made no reference to objective country documentation despite finding appellants credible; this is an error.
propositions.quote: In making these findings, the RPD made no reference to any objective country documentation, despite finding the Appellants credible. This constitutes an error.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found appellants credible but insufficient evidence of investigation; court finds RPD erred by ignoring objective country documentation.

propositions.text: Los Zetas cartel is powerful, involved in extortion, fuel theft, human smuggling, kidnapping, and operates in many Mexican states and Central/South America.
propositions.quote: The Los Zetas cartel is considered one of the most powerful organized crime groups in Mexico. They have amassed significant power to carry out an extractive business model-thus generating revenue from crimes, such as fuel theft, extortion, human smuggling and kidnapping, that are widely seen to inflict more suffering on the Mexican public than transnational drug trafficking. Los Zetas had a significant presence in several Mexican states on the Gulf (eastern) side of the country, and extended their reach to Ciudad Juárez (Chihuahua) and some Pacific states, and operate in Central and South America.

propositions.text: Los Zetas kill those who cannot pay extortion or refuse to work for them, often targeting migrants.
propositions.quote: Los Zetas are known to kill those who cannot pay extortion fees or who refuse to work for them, often targeting migrants.

propositions.text: Cartel del Noreste is a Los Zetas faction operating in Ecatepec, where appellants lived.
propositions.quote: The Cartel del Noreste is a faction of the Los Zetas. It operates in the Ecatepec region, where the Appellants were located.

propositions.text: Criminals target used car businesses for extortion with corrupt officials' help; extortion fees are known due to officials' knowledge; many extorted businessmen fled to Texas.
propositions.quote: Criminal organizations and cartels target used car businesses, like the PA's business, for extortion with the assistance of corrupt officials: Mexican criminals subsequently learned of the increased profits Mexican importers were receiving and began to extort them. The criminals required that the importers pay an extortion fee or "cuota" of $100 per imported car. With corrupt officials on their payroll, the criminals knew the exact (total) cuota to expect from the importers because they knew exactly how many cars had been imported on any given day. Since at least 2010, many of the Mexican businessmen who have been extorted and victimized by Mexican criminals reportedly fled their communities...only to resettle their families and businesses in various Texas cities on the U.S. side of the border. Many of these displaced Mexicans indicated that they had been victims of kidnapping, theft, assault, extortion, and other crimes by Mexican criminals who required them to pay thousands of dollars in exchange for the liberty to conduct business without reprisals, or in exchange for ransom demands.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Los Zetas powerful and violent, Cartel del Noreste operates where appellants lived, and criminals extort used car businesses with corrupt officials' help.

propositions.text: Individuals who report extortion do so at great personal risk.
propositions.quote: Individuals who complain or report extortion attempts do so at great personal risk.

propositions.text: Organized crime groups like Zetas in Tamaulipas act as insurgents, challenging legitimate governance and persecuting citizens.
propositions.quote: Organized crime groups such as the Zetas, specifically in the state of Tamaulipas, have evolved beyond mere criminal actors and are considered by some to be insurgents or threats to national security, in that they have continually challenged and/or opposed to legitimate institutions of governance. This is reflected by the fact that the Zetas and other groups are persecuting the people of the state of Tamaulipas, as well as other Mexican states, as they attempt to develop an alternate form of government in which criminality is the power that drives governance.

propositions.text: Mexican government is unable to control organized crime due to deep corruption, which has worsened over time.
propositions.quote: The Mexican government, whether at the municipal, state, or federal levels, has been unable to control organized crime due to the depth of corruption such groups have inserted into the political and governmental process, which has progressively gotten worse over time.

propositions.text: Corruption subjugates police forces to criminal elements, converting officers into surrogate organized crime actors involved in extortion, kidnapping, assassination.
propositions.quote: The culture of corruption in Mexican governmental entities, including public safety, political, and other institutional elements, has subjugated municipal, state, and federal police forces to criminal elements as a result of coercion, force, or death. Threats and acts of retribution convert police officers into surrogate organized crime actors who, in turn, participate in extortion, kidnapping, and assassination at the behest of their criminal sponsors.

propositions.text: Victims are those unwilling to participate in illicit activities; resistors face torture, death, or family victimization.
propositions.quote: The victims of these violent crimes are predominantly those citizens who are unwilling to participate in illicit activities. Failure to participate in corrupt practices routinely leads to the resistors being tortured or killed, or to the victimization of their extended family.

propositions.text: Various levels of Mexican government are incapable or unwilling to protect citizens and often collaborate with organized crime, becoming co-conspirators.
propositions.quote: It is far too obvious that various levels of government in Mexico are incapable or unwilling to protect its citizens and often collaborate with the organized crime groups to further their criminal endeavors, thereby becoming co-conspirators that are part of the problem and not the solution.

propositions.text: Mexican government is willfully blind and permissive of criminal activity, often partnering with criminal organizations.
propositions.quote: As a result, the Mexican government is willfully blind and permissive of criminal activity, and in many cases has become a partner in crime with several criminal organizations or cartels.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds reporting extortion is risky; Zetas act as insurgents; Mexican government is deeply corrupt, unable to control crime, and often collaborates with cartels.

propositions.text: Successful prosecution of corruption and crime in Mexico is extremely unlikely; impunity rate is 7%; crime is underreported due to mistrust in authorities.
propositions.quote: The US Country Reports 2016 indicates that Mexico has "extremely low rates of prosecution for all forms of crime," and prosecutions "could take years to complete" (7 Apr. 2017, 1, 9). Moloeznik indicates that the impunity rate for committed crimes is 7 percent (Moloeznik 29 June 2017). Sources indicate that crime is underreported due to generalized mistrust in authorities (ibid.; El Universal 21 June 2017).

paragraphs.summary: Court finds prosecutions in Mexico are rare and slow, impunity is high, and crime is underreported due to mistrust in authorities.

propositions.text: Los Zetas and associated cartels are powerful, extort used auto sales businesses, protected by corrupt officials; complaints are risky and unlikely to lead to prosecution; complainants likely to be murdered and family targeted.
propositions.quote: It is clear on the objective evidence that the Los Zetas and associated cartels are powerful, carry out extortion with respect to used auto sales business and are protected by police and corrupt government officials. Filing complaints about extortion is risky and unlikely to result in a prosecution. In addition, an individual who refuses to cooperate with extortion and files a formal complaint of extortion with the state police is very likely to lead to the individual being murdered and their family being targeted.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Los Zetas extort used auto businesses, are protected by corrupt officials, complaints are risky and likely lead to murder.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, cartel related to Los Zetas attempted to extort PA's business; PA refused, was threatened; PA filed complaint; appellants continue to be threatened because of complaint and refusal.
propositions.quote: I find, on a balance of probabilities, that a cartel related to the Los Zetas cartel attempted to extort the PA's used auto sales business. When he refused, he was subjected to threats against himself and his family. The PA filed a complaint about the extortion attempt with the assistance of his lawyer and the commander forwarded it for investigation. I find that the Appellants continue to be threatened by the cartel because the PA filed a complaint and refused to be extorted.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds cartel related to Los Zetas extorted PA's business, threats followed refusal and complaint, and threats continue.

propositions.text: Country documentation shows cartels can track people throughout Mexico using family networks, private investigators, property records, GPS trackers, and corrupt law enforcement.
propositions.quote: Country documentation indicates that individuals can be tracked throughout Mexico: 4.2 Ability of Cartels to Track People According to the Assistant Professor, cartels use family networks and private investigators to track people, as well as property records in the US and Mexico and placing GPS trackers on cars (Assistant Professor 28 May 2019). Similarly, Texas Monthly, a magazine covering issues such as politics, the environment, industry, and education (Texas Monthly n.d.), reports that an attorney with ties to drug cartel leaders, who had been providing information to the US government, was located by means including a GPS tracker on his car and cameras in his neighbourhood (Texas Monthly Oct. 2018). The Assistant Professor stated that a large debt or a personal vendetta could motivate a gang to track someone outside their area, and that gangs can use "corrupt law enforcement agents" to obtain information about people they pursue (Assistant Professor 1 Aug. 2019). Corroborating information could not be found among the sources consulted by the Research Directorate within the time constraints of this Response. The Assistant Professor stated that in order to extend their influence beyond their areas of operation, cartels rely on the "representation" they have in other areas (Assistant Professor 28 May 2019). For example, Justice in Mexico, a US-based initiative [housed at the Department of Political Science and International Relations at the University of San Diego (Justice in Mexico Apr. 2019)] that "works to improve citizen security, strengthen the rule of law, and protect human rights in Mexico" (Justice in Mexico 19 Mar. 2018, 28), reports that the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (Cartel Jalisco Nueva Generación, CJNG), a splinter group of the Sinaloa Cartel, has developed "strategic alliances" with groups in other regions, including Los Zetas and Gulf Cartel splinter groups along the Gulf Coast (Justice in Mexico 19 Mar. 2018, 1, 18-19). According to Insight Crime, Los Zetas have "made numerous temporary alliances" with Familia Michoacana and the BLO (InSight Crime 6 Apr. 2018). The US CRS report also notes that the BLO has alliances with "elements of Los Zetas" and that la Familia Michoacana was "[f]ormerly aligned with Los Zetas before the group's split from the Gulf [Cartel]" (US 3 July 2018, 19). [emphasis added] .... 5.4 Homicides Sources report an increase in the homicide rate (Forbes 6 Nov. 2018; Felbab-Brown Mar. 2019, 4; Justice in Mexico 19 Mar. 2018, 1), one cause of which is the splintering among criminal groups (Felbab-Brown Mar. 2019, 4) or disputes between factions (Forbes 6 Nov. 2018; Justice in Mexico 19 Mar. 2018, 1). Sources report that it is inexpensive for gangs to have someone killed in Mexico (International Crisis Group 15 June 2017; LA Times 30 Jan. 2019; Assistant Professor 28 May 2019): approximately US$100 (Assistant Professor 28 May 2019) or Drug cartels, including Los Zetas, the Gulf Cartel (Cartel del Golfo), La

paragraphs.summary: Country documentation shows cartels can track people across Mexico using networks, GPS, corrupt police, and have alliances; homicide rates are rising and killings are cheap.

propositions.text: Telecommunications companies in Mexico surrender user data to authorities 94% of the time, often without legal authority; Telmex/Telcel surrendered data 100% of requests.
propositions.quote: Telecommunications private data are available on request, without official authority: telecommunications companies received more than 145,000 requests for user data, out of which 94% of the times the information was surrendered, even when 30% of the requests were made by unidentified authorities or authorities that do not have a legal right to access user data requests. Moreover, the biggest telecommunications company (Telmex/Telcel) surrendered data 100% of the times authorities requested data (more than 116,000 requests)

paragraphs.summary: Telecommunications companies in Mexico surrender user data to authorities almost always, often without legal authority.

propositions.text: Country documentation is consistent with appellants' testimony that cartel could locate them anywhere in Mexico; regional cartels are volatile and police collusion is rampant.
propositions.quote: It is clear that the country documentation is consistent with the Appellants' testimony that the cartel could locate them anywhere in Mexico. Additional evidence indicates that regional cartels are volatile and alliances are difficult to track; also, police collusion with organized crime is rampant in Mexico.

paragraphs.summary: Country documentation supports appellants' testimony that cartels can locate them anywhere; cartels are volatile and police collusion is rampant.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, appellants could be located and harmed by cartel anywhere in Mexico.
propositions.quote: Based on the above noted country documentation and the credible testimony of the Appellants, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellants could be located and harmed by the cartel anywhere in Mexico.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds appellants could be located and harmed by cartel anywhere in Mexico on balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, PA and family face personalized risk in Mexico because of PA's refusal to be extorted and reporting; risk is personal, not general.
propositions.quote: I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the PA, and by extension his family, face a likelihood of personalized risk in Mexico. The cartel is after him because he refused to be extorted and reported the attempted extortion to state police. The reason for the harm is specific to the PA's actions. As such, it is personal in nature, and not a risk faced by the general public.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds PA and family face personal risk in Mexico due to PA's refusal and reporting; risk is personal, not general.

propositions.text: Appellants cannot avail themselves of state protection due to high official and police corruption and collusion with cartels in Mexico.
propositions.quote: Finally, based upon the same objective evidence referred to in the IFA analysis, I find that the Appellants could not avail themselves of state protection given the high level of official and police corruption, and collusion with cartels in Mexico.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds appellants cannot get state protection due to high corruption and collusion with cartels.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, appellants are persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, I have concluded that, on a balance of probabilities, the appellants are persons in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes appellants are persons in need of protection on balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: Appeal is allowed; I substitute my own decision that appellants are persons in need of protection under IRPA.
propositions.quote: The appeal is allowed. In accordance with subsection 111(1)(b), I substitute my own decision that the Appellants are persons in need of protection under subsection 97(1)(b) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: Court allows appeal and substitutes decision that appellants need protection under IRPA.
